Awesome
AW-sum
adjective / interjection (Gen X slang)
From awe (Old Norse agi, terror) + -some; in English since the 1590s for "full of awe, inspiring dread or reverence." The slang sense, "excellent, great, very cool," appears in California surf and teen speech in the late 1970s and became the Gen X superlative of the 1980s ("totally awesome," Fast Times at Ridgemont High, 1982; the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoon, 1987). By the 1990s it had flattened into the default American word of approval, applied to anything from a burrito to a parking space.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

For four centuries awesome meant that which fills a man with awe — the trembling reverence of a creature before something vastly greater than himself. Gen X turned it into a thumbs-up: an awesome concert, an awesome pizza, an awesome parking spot. The Christian observation is not that young people should never say it, but that the word was borrowed from a room only God rightly fills. Scripture’s word in the Authorized Version is terrible — "the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy" (Neh 1:5) — and its demand is not enthusiasm but reverence: "God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him" (Psa 89:7). "Let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him" (Psa 33:8). The writer to the Hebrews draws the line into the New Covenant: we serve God "acceptably with reverence and godly fear" (Heb 12:28). A generation that calls everything awesome will struggle to feel awe; the cure is not a word ban but a sight of God. Take a child under the night sky, or to Isaiah 6, and let him learn where the word came from: the holy, majestic, covenant-keeping God in Christ, before whom angels cover their faces.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X superlative (late 1970s–80s, from surf and Valley speech) for anything good; originally "inspiring awe" — a word borrowed from the reverence due to God alone (Psa 89:7).

expand to see more

AWESOME, adj. and interj. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–present) Excellent, great, very good; as an interjection, "Great!" "That ride was awesome." "Awesome, dude."

Intensified: totally awesome; awesome sauce (Millennial). By the 2000s the default American word of approval.

Original sense (1590s onward, still standard): inspiring awe; full of reverential fear or wonder.

Webster 1828: AWE, n. aw. [Gr. to be astonished.] 1. Fear mingled with admiration or reverence; reverential fear. Stand in awe and sin not. Psalms 4:4. 2. Fear; dread inspired by something great, or terrific.

Decode for parents: a generation that calls tacos awesome has to be taught that awe belongs first to the living God.

Key Scripture

Psa 89:7 — "God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him."

Neh 1:5 — "And said, I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments:"

Psa 33:8 — "Let all the earth fear the LORD: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him."

Psa 4:4 — "Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah."

Heb 12:28 — "Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:"

Modern Corruption

Awesome took the vocabulary of holy fear and handed it to pizza and parking spaces; Scripture reserves awe for the great and terrible God who keeps covenant and mercy.

expand to see more

The loss of awe. Words follow worship. When the culture’s highest word for wonder is applied to a burrito, it is a symptom that the culture has nothing left above the burrito to wonder at. The Psalmist’s command, "Stand in awe, and sin not" (Psa 4:4), connects reverence with holiness: men who fear God walk carefully. A people that has emptied awesome of God has, not by accident, also lost much of its fear of sinning.

Recovering the word. The church does not recover awe by policing adjectives; it recovers awe by showing the God of Isaiah 6, Exodus 19, and Revelation 1 — the God before whom John fell "as dead." Serve Him "with reverence and godly fear" (Heb 12:28). Children raised on that sight will still say awesome about their bikes, but they will know the difference between a good thing and the Holy One.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old Norse agi → English awe → awesome (1590s, inspiring reverent dread) → late-1970s surf/Valley slang → the default American "great."

expand to see more

Old Norse agi / Old English ege — terror, dread

Middle English awe — reverential fear

1590s awesome — full of awe; inspiring dread or wonder

Late 1970s–1980s California surf and Valley slang: excellent, very good

Scripture’s equivalent: terrible, fear, reverence (Neh 1:5; Psa 89:7)

Usage

""Dude, that wave was awesome!" — Huntington Beach, c. 1984."

"Pizza is good; only God is awesome in the old sense (Psa 89:7)."

"Stand in awe, and sin not (Psa 4:4) — the word’s first home."
